summary: Zhejiang University authors (ICSE 2026) define just-in-time Python type-annotation updating: given the old code, the new code and the old annotation of a parameter or return value, predict the new annotation. TypeUp chains three GPT-3.5-turbo prompts: select candidate types from project types collected by AST, explain retrieved similar historical code-type co-changes with chain-of-thought, then write the update. Retrieval uses CoditT5 embeddings over 36K co-change samples from 450 GitHub repos, limited to earlier commits. On a random 500-sample test split it produces 359 exact matches vs 253 for TypeGen (+41.9%). In a field test, 20 of 25 pull requests fixing Pyre-detected stale annotations in 10 projects were accepted (18 as-is, 2 after edits).

claims.claim: TypeUp outperforms the state-of-the-art type-inference approach TypeGen by 41.9%
claims.evidence: Table 2: 359 vs 253 correct annotations (+41.9%); exact-match precision .761 vs .682; recall .944 vs .742. Single run, one model, 500 samples. All baselines are type-inference tools that see only the post-change code, not the diff or the old annotation. Table 4's updating-prompt-only variant (no retrieval or reasoning stage) already reaches 303, so most of the margin over TypeGen comes from giving the model the diff and old type, not from TypeUp's retrieval design.

claims.claim: Each of the three LLM 'agents' contributes to performance
claims.evidence: Table 4 ablation: 303 (both removed), 328 and 334 (one removed), 359 (full), single run. Fig. 5 text reports exact-match precision of 0.471 with zero guiding examples, while Table 4 reports 0.701 with both the retrieval and reasoning stages removed. The paper does not explain this inconsistency, so it is unclear what the ablation actually removes.

claims.claim: Five retrieved guiding examples is the best setting
claims.evidence: Fig. 5 sweep over k on the test split itself; there is no validation split.

claims.claim: 20 of 25 generated updates were confirmed by developers
claims.evidence: Table 5: 18 merged, 2 merged after the authors rewrote them to PEP 604 style, 5 rejected. The 25 cases were preselected by Pyre warnings and manual review. Maintainers were not told the PRs were tool-generated.

claims.claim: Adding Pyre as a validator improves precision
claims.evidence: Table 6: exact-match precision .840 vs .761, but recall falls from .944 to .776 and correct annotations from 359 to 326. Pyre rejected some correct user-defined types and accepted some wrong ones.

patterns.note: Embedding retrieval of similar past code-type co-changes from the project history (with a temporal filter) raises exact-match precision from 0.471 at k=0 to 0.761 at k=5 (Fig. 5), and the ablation in Table 4 points the same way. Caveats: single model and run, k tuned on the test split, and the unexplained Fig. 5 vs Table 4 inconsistency.
Pyre as a post-hoc checker with up to five regenerate rounds trades coverage for precision: precision rises, but the number of correct updates falls from 359 to 326 (Table 6).

methodology.sample: 500 random test samples from 36,796 co-change samples (450 repos); field test on 25 stale annotations in 10 projects with >2k stars
methodology.baselines: pytype, Type4Py, HiTyper (on TypeGen), Tiger, TypeGen re-implemented on GPT-3.5-turbo; all infer types from post-change code only
methodology.models: GPT-3.5-turbo for all three stages; CoditT5 change encoder; Chroma vector store
methodology.ablations: Remove retrieval stage, reasoning stage, or both; k sweep; Pyre validator
methodology.contamination_controls: Retrieval restricted to earlier commits. GPT-3.5 pretraining overlap with public GitHub code is acknowledged but dismissed by comparison with TypeGen on the same model. The test split is random over the same repos as the knowledge base.

standards.artifacts: Replication package (code and dataset) claimed; the link is elided in the extracted text

biases.detail: Baselines solve a different task (type inference from current code) and never see the diff or the old annotation, which is the main input TypeUp adds.
Only GPT-3.5-turbo, a model that has since been retired.
One run; differences of 25-56 correct annotations out of 500 are reported without intervals.
The number of retrieved examples is chosen on the test split.
Public GitHub projects that are likely in GPT-3.5 training data; the TypeGen comparison does not rule out memorization triggered by the diff.
No token or API cost for the three-prompt chain.

verdict_reason: Peer-reviewed, with a sizeable dataset, a sensible temporal leakage control and a small real-PR field test. Against that: a single model and run, inference-only baselines that never see the diff, k tuned on the test split, an unexplained inconsistency between Fig. 5 and Table 4, and Python-only scope. Relevance to this discovery and onboarding round is low: it is about keeping Python type hints consistent with code.
applicability: Does not transfer directly. In Java, parameter and return types are compiler-checked, so stale signature types cannot persist the way Python hints can. The transferable idea is just-in-time co-change of documentation the compiler does not check, such as Javadoc @param/@return text, OpenAPI or JSON-schema contracts, and content-model docs shared across the repositories, using similar past co-changes from the team's own history as examples. The Pyre result is a caution for any such check: a static gate raised precision but lowered the number of correct updates, so surface these as review suggestions rather than blocking gates. This is a minor input to the knowledge-capture goal.
